issues.description: In Experiment 1 (and similarly Experiment 2) the mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects and no random effect for items or suffixes. Because 'condition' (adjective- vs noun-diagnostic) is a property that varies between only 20 suffixes (10 per condition), treating ~1,625 individual responses as independent observations is pseudoreplication. Without a by-suffix random intercept the standard error of the condition effect is underestimated and the p-value is anti-conservative. Notably, Experiment 3 DID include a by-suffix random intercept, making the omission in Experiments 1 and 2 inconsistent and likely inflating Type I error for the central effects.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: The verbal definition of type diagnosticity states the denominator is 'the total number of words falling into this category,' which would compute P(suffix | category). However, the worked example (-IAN = 0.54) and Appendix A (where the three category diagnosticities for each suffix sum to 1) make clear that the quantity actually computed is P(category | suffix) — i.e., the denominator must be the total number of words ending in that suffix, not the total number of words in the category. The Methods description therefore contradicts the actual computation, harming replicability.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: In the eye-tracking experiment the number of words preceding the target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs 5.23). Target position in a sentence systematically affects exactly the measures that showed effects (go-past time, regressions-out), because later-positioned targets accrue more preceding text to which the eyes can regress and more opportunity for integration cost. The authors note the difference but do not control for it (e.g., by entering word position as a covariate), so the key congruency effects may be partly or wholly attributable to this confound.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: Experiment 1 presents nonwords visually and concludes readers 'extract information about lexical category from written language.' However, skilled readers automatically phonologically recode print, and prior work cited by the authors (Onnis & Christiansen, 2008) shows word-final phonemes themselves cue lexical category almost as well as suffixes. Because the orthographic suffixes co-vary with their phonological realisations, Experiment 1 cannot dissociate orthography-specific knowledge from phonological cues. Only Experiment 2 holds phonology constant. The strong conclusion that the effect reflects written-language knowledge is therefore not warranted by Experiment 1 alone.
issues.quote: Results suggest that skilled readers extract information about lexical category from written language.

issues.description: The stated feedforward hypothesis is the reverse of the construct definitions and of the actual experimental design. Diagnosticity is defined as spelling-to-meaning consistency (reading direction) and specificity as meaning-to-spelling consistency (production direction), yet here diagnosticity is said to impact spelling production and specificity to impact print-to-meaning reading. The experiments actually do the opposite (diagnosticity drives the categorisation/reading experiments; specificity drives the spelling experiment), and the later 'Experiments' section states the correct mapping. This is a direct internal contradiction that confuses the theoretical logic.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

issues.subcategory: overinterpretation of trivial effect / regression attenuation
issues.description: The central claim that writing conveys more category information than speech rests on a mean entropy difference of just 0.02 bits (0.61 vs 0.63) and a regression slope of 0.9 'significantly different from 1.' First, a 0.02-bit difference is practically negligible despite statistical significance. Second, inferring 'spelling is more predictive' from a slope below 1 is statistically problematic: measurement/estimation error in the predictor (H_phonology) attenuates regression slopes toward 0, so a slope <1 could be an artifact of regression dilution rather than genuine asymmetry. A paired comparison of H values per suffix would be the appropriate test, and the effect size is too small to support the strong conclusions drawn.
issues.quote: the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.description: Throughout the paper (including the title and repeated references to 'spelling-to-meaning' regularities) the construct of 'meaning' is operationalised solely as lexical category (noun/adjective/verb). Lexical/syntactic category is a grammatical property, not semantic meaning in the conventional sense; equating the two is a substantial conceptual leap. The citation to Baayen et al. (2011) acknowledges this is only 'a similar conceptualisation,' but the paper consistently generalises claims about 'meaning' and the transmission of 'meaningful information' from what is actually a category-marking result.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of “meaning”).

issues.description: Experiment 3 examined six eye-movement measures (skips, first fixation, first run dwell, go-past, regressions-in, regressions-out) with no correction for multiple comparisons, and the authors explicitly state they had no concrete predictions about which measures would be affected. Reporting two significant effects out of six at uncorrected p<.05 risks inflated familywise error, and the selective interpretation of go-past and regressions-out as 'late integration' effects is post hoc.
issues.quote: we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures (that characterise skips, fixations, reading time, and regressions; see Rayner et al., 2004; Warren et al., 2009).

issues.description: The token-based interaction is reported as 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01.' A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to p ≈ 0.55 and cannot be associated with p < 0.01. This is either a typographical error or an error in the analysis, and as reported it is uninterpretable, undermining confidence in the token-based specificity result.
issues.quote: (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as 0.86% ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%, which (taken literally) would indicate near-zero performance. This is clearly a units error (should be 86%, 66–98%), but as printed it is a reporting error that affects the credibility of the manipulation check and editorial care of the statistics.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: None of the three experiments report an a priori power analysis or any justification for sample size (N = 46, 29, 47). Experiment 2, with only 29 participants and 11 suffixes, is particularly underpowered for detecting a specificity-by-condition interaction. Absence of sample-size planning limits confidence in null results (e.g., the several null eye-tracking measures) and in the robustness of the graded effects.
issues.quote: Participants. Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.

issues.description: All three experiments use exclusively nonwords, yet the conclusions are framed as general claims about skilled reading of English and the function of the writing system. Nonword processing (especially when participants are told every sentence contains a nonword) recruits decoding and guessing strategies that differ from natural reading of real words. The leap from nonword behaviour to claims about how the writing system serves real reading is not directly validated.
issues.quote: Three psychological experiments tested skilled readers’ knowledge and exploitation of the relationship between suffix spelling and lexical category.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly advances a strong functional-evolutionary claim that English spelling 'became fractionated' or 'evolved' to 'maximise the transmission of meaningful information.' This adaptationist framing attributes purpose to an orthographic system on the basis of correlational corpus statistics and a single secondary diachronic source (Berg & Aronoff) covering only four suffixes. Such teleological claims are not supported by the present data and risk being mistaken for demonstrated mechanisms.
issues.quote: We close by arguing that English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.subcategory: order/fatigue confound and undocumented prior task
issues.description: Experiment 1 was run at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session. The nature of the prior task is not described, raising the possibility of carryover, priming, or fatigue effects, and making it impossible to evaluate whether the preceding session influenced performance. This also complicates replication.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.description: Experiment 1 used a 2-second timeout despite instructions not emphasising speed, and 11.7% of data points were lost to timeouts or invalid responses. If timeouts occur disproportionately on harder/less diagnostic items, the missingness is non-random and could bias the diagnosticity gradient analyses. No analysis of the pattern of missingness is reported.
issues.quote: (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: The go-past congruency effect is reported in the text as B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001, but Table 5 lists the estimate as 43 with t = 3.76. These discrepancies between the narrative and the table indicate transcription errors and reduce confidence in the precision of the reported statistics.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) such that go-past times were longer for incongruent trials than for congruent ones.

issues.description: A large proportion of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of exactly 1, and the means are very high (0.78 and 0.82). This heavy ceiling clustering restricts variance in the predictors used for the 'graded' analyses, meaning the graded effects are effectively driven by a small number of low-value suffixes. This limits the strength of the claim that behavioural sensitivity 'mirrors' a continuous gradient, and makes the graded analyses sensitive to a few influential items.
issues.quote: It is immediately apparent that a substantial number of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of 1.

issues.description: Both diagnosticity and specificity were computed using only the single most frequent pronunciation of each suffix. Many suffixes have multiple pronunciations, and collapsing to one realisation can mischaracterise the sound-to-spelling mapping (the very relationship the constructs are meant to capture), potentially biasing specificity values for suffixes with variable phonology.
issues.quote: Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix.

issues.subcategory: researcher degrees of freedom in exploratory analyses
issues.description: The 'Why are some suffixes more diagnostic' section involves multiple data-contingent decisions: removing 7 suffixes below 0.35, then 40 suffixes at diagnosticity = 1, after which the sign of the correlation reverses (from -0.24 to +0.23). Similar selective exclusions (20 and 29 suffixes, then all with specificity = 1) are made for specificity. These post-hoc, outcome-dependent exclusions inflate the chance of finding 'significant' correlations and are not corrected for multiple testing; they should be treated as exploratory only.
issues.quote: Once we remove these 40 suffixes, a positive correlation is observed (0.23, p < 0.05), meaning that highly diagnostic suffixes tend to be those that occur in many words.

issues.description: The diagnosticity-by-congruency interaction on go-past time is interpreted as showing the effect is carried by the incongruent condition, but the incongruent-condition simple effect is non-significant (p = 0.13) and is described as a 'trend.' Interpreting a p = 0.13 result as evidence of an effect overstates the data, especially given the small number of suffixes contributing to the gradient.
issues.quote: whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13).

issues.subcategory: congruency confounded with context template per suffix
issues.description: In Experiment 2 each suffix's congruent and incongruent conditions correspond to two specific, different sentence-template/category types (e.g., for -OUS, congruent = adjective context, incongruent = noun context). Thus within a suffix the congruency manipulation is perfectly confounded with which sentence template is used, and a 'congruency effect' could reflect template-specific syntactic/semantic biasing rather than stored knowledge of suffix specificity per se. The design does not fully isolate the suffix-category knowledge it aims to test.
issues.quote: For each suffix’s target spelling two context types were selected – one that was congruent with the category that this spelling denoted and one that was incongruent with it.

issues.description: The strong claim that spellings 'have changed in such a way as to express meaningful information more strongly' is supported only by Berg & Aronoff's analysis of a handful of suffixes (and a single example, glorius→glorious). Generalising a system-wide functional evolution of English orthography from such limited diachronic data is speculative and not supported by the authors' own (synchronic) corpus analysis.
issues.quote: This hypothesis is supported by diachronic data on the evolution of suffix spellings from Old English to modern days provided by Berg and Aronoff (2017).

issues.description: Experiment 3 is described as a 'more natural sentence reading task,' but participants were explicitly warned that every sentence contained a nonword. This expectation likely changes reading strategy (heightened attention to and processing of the target region), undermining the claim of naturalness and the generalisation of the integration-cost effects to ordinary reading.
issues.quote: Participants were warned that each sentence would contain a nonword and were asked to read for comprehension.
